titre_video: The Man Who Smoked Weed for 10 Years

segments.titre: Alex, the "high-functioning stoner", and the 10-year THC autopsy
segments.resume: Alex believes a little weed never killed anyone and sees himself as the ultimate high-functioning stoner after a decade of daily use that began as a way to relax after work. His brain has deployed a defense mechanism that altered his biology, and the video presents a year-by-year biological autopsy of 3,650 days of THC.
segments.texte: “A little weed now and again never killed anyone.” At least, that’s what Alex thinks as he lights up every day. What started as a way to relax after a long workday has spiralled into a decade long habit. But Alex thinks he’s fine. He considers himself as the ultimate “high-functioning stoner”. What he didn’t realize is that his brain is panicking. To survive the daily chemical flood, it has deployed a defense mechanism that has fundamentally altered his biology. What happens in the human body after you flood it with THC for 3,650 days straight? This is the year-by-year biological autopsy of a 10 year habit, and how a “natural” plant rewires a human life.

segments.titre: Year zero: stress, daily smoking and the reward system downregulation
segments.resume: Alex, 22, lands a high-pressure corporate job and starts smoking weed daily to take the edge off, relax, calm his racing mind and sleep. His brain begins to retreat from the constant THC overstimulation by downregulating its reward system, compared to a city turning off parts of its power grid to prevent a surge.
segments.texte: 22 year old Alex has just stepped into the corporate world. He’s a high achiever, landing an intense, high pressure position straight out of college. But the long hours and relentless workload start to stress him out pretty quickly. He used to smoke weed once in a while, but now he starts smoking daily to take the edge off. It relaxes him, stops his mind from racing and helps him sleep. It’s win win… or so he thinks. But beneath the surface, the neuro-hijack has begun. To protect itself from constant overstimulation, his brain starts retreating. His reward system is slowly downregulated, something his brain deems necessary to survive the tsunami of THC bombarding it every day. Like a city turning off sections of its power grid to prevent a massive surge, Alex’s brain is altering its own baseline just to keep the lights on. How much of that grid is about to go dark… forever?

segments.titre: Year one: lost hobbies, gym motivation, irritability and fewer dreams
segments.resume: In his first year of daily use Alex still performs well at work and looks like a high-functioning stoner, but stops playing guitar, loses his creative drive and drops his gym routine from 3-4 times a week to none. He wakes up cranky and tired even after full nights of sleep and has fewer dreams without knowing why.
segments.texte: It’s year one of his habit. Alex is going through life working hard, seeing his friends, and even getting an excellent performance review. He’s truly a “high functioning stoner”. But things are starting to change in his life in ways he’s not even realizing. Throughout college, he loved playing his guitar in the evenings, but he hasn’t touched it in months. He’s just not in the mood. The creative drive is gone. He also used to hit the gym 3 to 4 times a week, but after starting his daily habit, his motivation tanked. The workouts dropped to twice a week, then once, then stopped all together. Alex thinks it’s because of the long hours he’s working and lack of energy. And he’s getting irritable. Even when he gets a full night’s sleep, he wakes up feeling a little cranky and tired. He’s having fewer dreams, but he doesn’t know why that is… not yet.

segments.titre: Tolerance builds fast: the medical marijuana study
segments.resume: By the end of the first year Alex smokes more than ever because tolerance forces larger amounts of THC to reach a baseline relaxed state. A medical marijuana study found patients got 0.5% less relief with each session, a 10% reduction after 20 sessions, so tolerance in daily users builds in weeks, not years.
segments.texte: By the end of the first year, Alex is smoking more weed than he ever did. His system has built up a tolerance. Now needs larger amounts of THC just to get to a baseline relaxed state. Doctors administering medical marijuana recently found out just how fast that tolerance builds up. One study found that patients experienced 0.5% less relief with each session of medical marijuana. It might sound tiny, but after 20 sessions it adds up to a 10% reduction in symptom relief. For someone using weed daily, that means their tolerance to weed builds up in a matter of weeks. Not years. While Alex isn’t using marijuana medically, he is using it to soothe his symptoms of anxiety and stress. But now, it's just not doing the job like it used to. So he smokes more frequently.

segments.titre: Cannabis Use Disorder: 30% of daily users
segments.resume: In his second and third years of daily use Alex socializes less and has unknowingly become one of the 30% of daily users who develop Cannabis Use Disorder (CUD). CUD means compulsively continuing to use marijuana despite adverse effects on daily life, mental health and physical wellbeing, and chronic daily smokers are at especially high risk.
segments.texte: In his second and third years of daily use, Alex is socializing outside his house less and less. Because Alex has unknowingly become one of the 30% of daily users who develop Cannabis Use Disorder, or CUD. Because he’s a chronic daily smoker, he’s at especially high risk for the disorder. CUD means someone who compulsively continues to use marijuana despite it having adverse effects on their daily life, mental health and physical wellbeing.

segments.titre: Withdrawal restlessness, driving high and social drift
segments.resume: When Alex skips weed during an evening out he is visibly restless and fixated on returning home to light up, so he finds ways to smoke while out and takes the risk of driving high. By the start of his third year he sees friends far less and drifts away from anyone who does not just smoke weed.
segments.texte: The few times Alex has been out with friends all evening and skipped smoking weed, he’s visibly restless. He’s just fixated on getting back to his place and lighting up. So as the year goes on, he decides he’s going to find a way to smoke weed while out and about. Even though he’s getting into his car later; he’ll take the risk of driving high. Eventually, at the start of his third year of daily use, Alex is seeing his friends way less than he used to. He’s starting to drift away from anyone who doesn’t want to just hang out and smoke weed.

segments.titre: Memory loss and amotivational syndrome
segments.resume: By the end of the third year Alex wonders if he has ADHD because his working and short-term memory is failing, he misses deadlines and does not care. What he thinks is corporate burnout is actually amotivational syndrome, a devastating drop in everyday drive caused by sustained daily cannabis use.
segments.texte: By the end of the year, Alex is wondering if he has ADHD. His working memory is cratering. He’s missing critical deadlines at work because the due date vanished from his mind. He’s failing to complete tasks he said he’d personally take care of. His short term memory is wiping the second he takes them on. But the truth is, he doesn’t really care. Alex is bored at work and doesn’t feel like doing anything work related some days. What he thinks is corporate burnout is actually something called “amotivational syndrome”. Sustained daily cannabis use results in a devastating drop in everyday drive.

segments.titre: Dopamine, the reward center and the college student study
segments.resume: THC causes a dopamine surge and rewards the brain without real-world effort, hardwiring it to abandon non-weed sources of fulfillment. A 4-year study of college students doing tasks for money showed the heaviest weed users had decreased reward-center activity when anticipating rewards, and over time weed blunts dopamine production so hobbies, social life and work give less reward.
segments.texte: When THC enters Alex’s system, it causes a surge of dopamine. It hijacks his brain and gives him the feeling of contentment. By using weed daily, Alex is rewarding his brain repeatedly without expending an ounce of real world effort. He’s hardwiring his brain to abandon any non-weed sources of fulfillment. To confirm this, scientists ran a 4 year study on college students. They forced subjects to perform a series of simple tasks for financial reward. Meanwhile, researchers were imaging their brains in real time to see the fallout. Students who were using weed the most had decreased activity in their reward center when anticipating their money at the end of the task set. Scientists concluded, “as cannabis alters the brain’s reward center, regular users begin to anticipate less reward from non-cannabis sources.” That’s why Alex’s desire to put in effort for any other tasks that can cause a dopamine surge – like achieving a personal goal - has gone out the window. Over time, weed blunts the brain’s dopamine production. Even if Alex got back into his hobbies or social life, he would receive less dopamine as a reward. It’s part of the reason Alex isn’t that interested in leaving his house or why he just doesn’t care about his job.

segments.titre: Self-medicating anxiety: long-term effects opposite to short-term effects
segments.resume: Instead of quitting, Alex increases his weed intake, believing career stress worsens his anxiety and that weed is his only escape. In fact, daily cannabis use can worsen anxiety, depression and emotional distress, and the long-term effects of chronic marijuana use are the opposite of its short-term results.
segments.texte: But instead of quitting, Alex ups his weed intake. He’s convinced that all the stress from his career is making his anxiety worse. Weed is his only escape. At least, that’s what he thinks. In fact, daily cannabis use can take a toll on mental health, leading to symptoms like worsening anxiety, depression, or general emotional distress. Many people start using weed daily to self-medicate and deal with these issues. But over time, frequent THC use will only exacerbate them. Why? Because the long-term effects of chronic marijuana use are actually the opposite of its short-term results.

segments.titre: Sleep and REM suppression: why weed makes anxiety worse
segments.resume: Low doses of weed work like a sedative in the short term, but with long-term and increasing use the effect on sleep reverses, as with prolonged alcohol use. THC binds to brain receptors that suppress REM sleep, when the brain clears cellular waste, processes stress, sharpens working memory and lowers stress hormones, so Alex's anxiety flares up.
segments.texte: That’s most obvious when it comes to sleep. Plenty of people use weed before bed to help unwind and sleep more easily. In the short term, low doses of marijuana work like a sedative. People fall asleep faster and stay asleep longer. But after long term and increasing use, the effects on sleep are reversed. Just like with prolonged alcohol use. Because while Alex is taking weed to help him relax and sleep, he doesn’t know that THC binds to brain receptors that specifically suppress the REM stage. That’s when the brain clears out a lot of its cellular waste to reset for the next day. And Alex’s brain? It’s not doing that as much as it should. It’s like running a computer for years without ever clearing the cache or updating the OS. Things are going to get backed up and slower. REM sleep not only helps the brain process stressful events, sharpen working memory, and strengthen brain cell connections; it also lowers stress hormones and supports mental health in general. The less REM sleep Alex gets, the more he feels some low-level stress in his system… even when he doesn’t know why. Which is why his anxiety is flaring up. Alex traded in better overall mental health and stress levels for temporary stress relief.

segments.titre: Years four and five: cravings and declining work performance
segments.resume: In his fourth and fifth years Alex cannot skip a day without cravings, and use shifts from evenings to early afternoon and some weekend mornings. His performance declines, his boss stops giving him bigger responsibilities, and complex decision-making becomes increasingly hard.
segments.texte: And he didn’t even know it. Things get worse in his fourth and fifth year of daily use. At this point, Alex can’t skip a day of weed use without feeling cravings. Evening weed use has moved up to early afternoon use and on the weekends, occasional morning use as well. His work performance is rapidly declining. His boss has stopped giving him some of the bigger responsibilities he used to. Partly because Alex doesn’t seem as interested in a promotion anyway. And partly because it’s increasingly hard for Alex to deal with complex decision-making.

segments.titre: CB1 receptor downregulation and grey matter loss
segments.resume: THC attaches to CB1 receptors, and the brain responds by downregulating their number and availability by up to 20%, especially in regions like the medial temporal cortex, insula and orbitofrontal cortex. Grey matter reduction, mainly in the hippocampus and orbitofrontal cortex, impairs decision making, reward processing, social norms and responses to adversity, and may relate to Alex's lack of motivation.
segments.texte: Because at this point Alex is actively losing grey matter. THC, the main active ingredient in cannabis, attaches to cannabinoid type 1 – CB1 – receptors in the brain. When these receptors are overwhelmed, the brain begins a survival shutdown. It down-regulates the number and availability of active CB1 receptors by up to 20%. CB1 receptors are scattered all throughout the brain; though they congregate in heavy concentrations in critical regions. These include the medial temporal cortex, temporal pole, insula, and orbitofrontal cortex. For the non-neuroscientists among us, these are the areas that deal with motivational, emotional, and affective processing. The reduction in receptors triggers a reduction of grey matter in these regions. While research is still too limited to show how much grey matter decreases, we know the hippocampus and orbitofrontal cortex are the most affected. The hippocampus is responsible for important human survival traits like decision making, processing rewards and reading social norms. It also controls how someone responds to adversity. That probably explains why Alex can’t handle complex tasks at work anymore. As these brain regions shrink, Alex’s ability to weigh options and decide begins to suffer. He can’t predict the potential results of decisions like he used to. His lack of motivation might also be correlated with his hippocampus decreasing in volume.

segments.titre: IQ loss, executive function and why "high-functioning stoner" is a lie
segments.resume: A New Zealand study of more than 1,000 people over 38 years found long-term weed smokers lost 5-6 IQ points over time, with the greatest impairments in executive functioning and processing speed. Alex's blunted management center plus amotivational syndrome creates a vicious cycle of getting less done and needing more time, which makes the term high-functioning stoner a lie.
segments.texte: What does this result in? A radical shift in his behavior. And Alex’s belief that he’s a “high functioning stoner” is about to shatter. Even if his colleagues can’t tell he’s high, daily weed use is still influencing every single aspect of his life. And it’s starting to make long-term changes in his brain structure and performance. Scientists in New Zealand studied more than 1,000 participants over 38 years, dividing them into never-smokers, and then by frequency of weed use. Their research shows that people who were long term smokers experienced a drop of 5-6 IQ points. Not that they were 5 IQ points lower than their non-smoker peers. They actually lost IQ over years of habitual weed use. While this decrease in IQ was evident across the board, another study found that the “greatest impairments were for the domains of executive functioning and processing speed.” The former being the “management center” of the brain. The part that motivates you to plan, set, and execute goals; the latter is the amount of time your brain needs to take in information, make sense of it, and act accordingly. Since Alex’s management center is a little blunted, together with his “amotivational syndrome”, it’s creating a vicious cycle. He’s getting less and less done… but needs more time to do it all. Which is why the term “high functioning stoner” is a lie.

segments.titre: The myth that weed is harmless: DARE, decriminalization and perception shift
segments.resume: Marijuana was demonized for a long time by teachers, parents and DARE officers with unrealistic dangers, and when it was decriminalized or legalized the scare tactics were exposed and the pendulum swung toward believing it is not harmful. In 2002 about 50% of people thought smoking marijuana was harmful versus 33% in 2014, even as potency became 4 times higher.
segments.texte: Alex doesn’t realize this yet. The effects have accumulated slowly over time and he has bought into the myth that weed has zero harmful effects. Marijuana was overly demonized and lied about for a very long time. Everyone from schoolteachers and parents to local DARE officers would warn about ridiculous - and unrealistic sounding - “dangers” of weed to scare students into never trying it. However, when marijuana was decriminalized or even legalized in some states, it became clear these scare tactics weren’t true. The pendulum then swung to the other side, and people started believing marijuana wasn’t bad for you at all. In 2002, around 50% of people thought smoking marijuana was harmful. In 2014, that number had dropped to 33%. Even as it became 4 times more potent, and people became more aware about the dangers of substance abuse, marijuana mostly gets a free pass. But by the sixth and seventh years of weed use,

segments.titre: Lung damage: smoke is smoke
segments.resume: By years six and seven Alex develops a chronic cough even when not smoking; the myth that weed smoke is unlike tobacco is wrong. The American Lung Association says marijuana smoke contains toxins and carcinogens similar to tobacco, killing defensive lung cells and causing chronic cough, phlegm, wheeze, bronchitis, air pockets and, per CT scans, airway thickening, inflammation and emphysema.
segments.texte: it’s not just Alex’s brain experiencing changes. He is starting to notice physical symptoms. Coughing while smoking weed is entirely normal and expected. But Alex has developed a chronic cough, whether he’s smoking or not. There’s a persistent myth that smoking weed is not harmful to users, unlike tobacco. But smoke is smoke. Inhaling it frequently, no matter what’s in it, will damage a person’s respiratory system. The American Lung Association found that “...although not as carcinogenic… marijuana smoke contains toxins and carcinogens similar to those in tobacco smoke.” In heavy smokers, weed use has caused air pockets in between the lungs, as well as in the lungs themselves. The smoke kills the lung’s defensive cells, the ones that remove dust and germs, making them more vulnerable to infection. This leads to symptoms like chronic cough, phlegm production, wheeze, and acute bronchitis. CT scans have shown that people who only smoke marijuana had “greater airway thickening and inflammation as well as emphysema compared to both nonsmokers and tobacco-only smokers”.

segments.titre: Bullous lung disease and lung problems at age 41
segments.resume: Marijuana smokers face significantly higher risks of bullous lung disease, where air gets trapped and damages the lungs, partly because they inhale more and hold smoke up to 4 times longer than cigarette smoke. Marijuana users develop lung problems at an average age of 41, compared with 65 for tobacco smokers.
segments.texte: It’s a turning point in Alex’s future. One study found that marijuana smokers face significantly higher risks of developing conditions like bullous lung disease. This is where air gets trapped in the lungs and damages them, making breathing difficult. Researchers think that it’s because people who smoke weed tend to inhale a lot more. They also hold the smoke in their lungs for up to 4 times longer than cigarette smoke. The most surprising part of weed users’ lung conditions is the age at which they get them. While tobacco smokers developed lung problems at an average age of 65, marijuana users developed lung problems at an average age of 41 Alex is running out of time.

segments.titre: Edibles and the cardiovascular risk: heart attack and stroke
segments.resume: In his eighth year Alex switches to edibles to spare his lungs, but new research shows any form of weed raises the risk of heart attack and stroke. Daily users had 25% higher odds of a heart attack and 42% higher odds of stroke, and men under 55 and women under 65 had a 36% combined increase in coronary heart disease, heart attack or stroke, even among those who never used tobacco or e-cigarettes.
segments.texte: By the eighth year, Alex is tired of coughing all the time and coming down with colds and bronchitis. So he decides to get his weed fix in other ways. That means more edibles than joints. Maybe that will help his lungs recover. And they might - especially the more he reduces his use - but this form of weed use carries its own risks. Scientists recently found that any form of weed use led to potential health problems that have nothing to do with the brain and lungs. New research discovered that frequent weed users are at significantly increased risk of heart attacks and strokes. The risk to Alex is no longer just cognitive. It’s a physical threat in his chest. Daily users had 25% higher odds of having a heart attack. Even worse, they increased their chance of stroke by 42%. To make sure the results were accurate, researchers controlled for tobacco use among participants, since many people smoke both weed and cigarettes. But the evidence was still there. For men under 55 and women under 65, weed use resulted in a 36% combined increase for coronary heart disease, heart attack or stroke. And as the study put it, “the odds were higher even when researchers looked only at those who had never used tobacco products or e-cigarettes”. Switching from smoking to eating may take care of Alex’s lungs. But it’s still killing his cardiovascular system.

segments.titre: Alex decides to quit: is the damage reversible?
segments.resume: After a couple more years of use, with work suffering and friends distant, Alex hears about the heart attack study and decides to quit. He faces the scariest question: whether the damage to his mind and body is reversible or his baseline is permanently altered after ten years, and the answer is that it depends.
segments.texte: After a couple more years of marijuana use, Alex has had enough. His work has suffered, he feels disconnected from a lot of his friends and he wants to make a change. He finally hears about the heart attack study and makes a decision: it’s time for him to quit. But that’s when the scariest question of all pops up. Is the damage weed has done to his mind and body…reversible? Or is his baseline permanently altered after his brain and heart have spent ten years in chemical stasis? The answer is…it depends.

segments.titre: Cognitive recovery after quitting and the age of onset factor
segments.resume: One study found heavy users and recent quitters did worse on IQ, processing speed and memory, but returned to pre-drug performance after 3 months of abstinence. A study of over 1,000 subjects found rebound depends on the age they started: Alex began as an adult, while cessation did not fully restore brain functioning in those who started in their teens because the teenage brain is still developing.
segments.texte: One study found that heavy marijuana users, and even those who had just quit, did worse in IQ, processing speed, immediate, and delayed memory. But after 3 months of quitting weed, they were back to their “pre-drug performance” when it came to their cognitive abilities. But that comes with a caveat. Because another study that looked at over 1,000 subjects found that whether you rebounded or not had a lot to do with one factor. The age at which they started smoking. Here, Alex has something good going for him. He hadn’t even tried weed until his last year of college. And he didn’t become a daily user until he was almost 23. If he had started as a teenager, that might be a different story. The large-scale study found that “cessation of cannabis use did not fully restore neuropsychological [brain] functioning” among people who started in their teens. The teenage brain is still morphing and developing. Reducing grey matter and otherwise messing with CB1 receptors in a brain that’s constantly changing causes much more damage than to an adult. But in adults, CB1 receptors can return to

segments.titre: CB1 receptors recover, then insomnia and vivid dreams
segments.resume: In adults CB1 receptors can return to normal levels four weeks after weed use stops, about how long THC metabolites stay in a daily user's system, so Alex is in the clear brain-wise, though heavy long use means a longer recovery. He will have insomnia and then unusually vivid dreams as his REM cycle returns with a bang.
segments.texte: normal levels even just four weeks after weed use stops. In daily users, that’s about how long THC metabolites remain in the system. So Alex is in the clear when it comes to his brain. Even though because of the duration and frequency of his use, it will probably take him a lot more time to get back to his baseline than for a more “social” user. He will also suffer through a period of insomnia and sleep difficulty. Because he was relying on weed to sleep for so long, he will also experience weirdly, particularly vivid dreams. Experts think that’s because Alex’s full REM cycle will come back with a bang, leading to intense dreaming.

segments.titre: Recovery of the lungs: reversible inflammation, modest lung function gains
segments.resume: Doctors say airway inflammation and bronchitis induced by cannabis are largely reversible, and those who quit were no more likely to have cough or sputum than people who never smoked. Alex is back at the gym, but objective lung function changes after quitting weed are more modest than after tobacco cessation, and there is not enough research to explain why.
segments.texte: What about Alex’s lungs? And perhaps most importantly, his heart? Well, doctors who treat those who quit smoking weed and/or tobacco say that “the airway inflammation and bronchitis induced by cannabis are largely reversible”. When doctors followed up with those who quit, they were no more likely to have symptoms like coughing, sputum, or other respiratory symptoms than those who never smoked at all. That’s great news for Alex. He’s back at the gym, and slowly finding it easier to do his old exercises than at any point in the past 10 years. But his lung function underneath all that hasn’t rebounded as much as he’d hoped. One source found that after quitting weed, “objective lung function changes are more modest than with tobacco cessation”. One could argue that’s because tobacco damages the lungs a lot more to begin with; but there’s just not enough research to know for sure.

segments.titre: Heart recovery: what we don't know
segments.resume: Alex's heart condition is the most important unknown: quitting leads to some improvement in cardiovascular health, as with most substances. But because marijuana was illegal for so long, many long-term effects on the heart have not been studied.
segments.texte: Which touches on the most important part of Alex’s health after quitting: his heart condition. Unfortunately, this is one area where we just don’t know the answer. As with most substances, quitting leads to some improvement in his cardiovascular health. But since marijuana was illegal for so long, many long-term effects haven’t been studied.

segments.titre: Outlook for Alex and outro on dreams
segments.resume: Alex's motivation is back, he feels more emotionally regulated and can run a few miles, and his body and mind seem likely to be alright after a few difficult months of detox. One part may be a literal nightmare, and the narrator points viewers to the video "What Happens to Your Dreams When You Smoke Weed".
mots_cles: What Happens to Your Dreams When You Smoke Weed
segments.texte: Overall though, things are looking up for Alex. His motivation is back, he feels more emotionally regulated, he can run a few miles without any issues…and it seems like his body and mind are going to be alright. Alex is going to face a few difficult months while he detoxes… but one part might be a literal nightmare. Watch ‘What Happens to Your Dreams When You Smoke Weed’ to see what goes on at night.
